title: Call Abandonment Rate: What It Is, How to Calculate It, and What Counts as Normal | Blog
summary: Call abandonment rate is the percentage of inbound callers who hang up before receiving help. Learn the formula, benchmarks, causes, and how to reduce it.
body_markdown:
Of all the numbers on a contact center dashboard, call abandonment rate is one of the quietest. When a customer gives up in the queue, there’s no complaint, angry survey, or escalation. On a support line, this means a problem left unsolved. On a sales line, it’s a customer who was ready to buy, and decided the wait wasn’t worth it.


Most contact centers track abandonment, but not everyone knows what a good number looks like, whether their definition matches anyone else’s, or how much revenue they’re losing as a result. This guide covers it all: what call abandonment rate measures, how to calculate it accurately, and what counts as normal. As a bonus, we’ll share how Omaha Steaks brought theirs from 16% down to 2%. In December alone, every percentage point for them signals $1 million of revenue lost.


## What is call abandonment rate?


**Call abandonment rate** is the percentage of inbound calls where the caller hangs up before reaching someone who can help them. It’s one of the clearest signals of whether a contact center has enough capacity to meet demand. When the rate climbs, callers are telling you that the wait cost more than their problem was worth.


A call counts as abandoned whether the caller gives up in the queue, on hold, or partway through an IVR menu. How teams count each of those is the biggest discrepancy in how contact centers calculate abandonment. Two contact centers with the same performance often report very different numbers.


## How to calculate call abandonment rate


The formula is simple:


**Call abandonment rate = (abandoned calls ÷ total inbound calls) × 100**


Say your line takes 2,000 calls on a Monday and 120 callers hang up before being answered. Your abandonment rate is 120 ÷ 2,000 × 100 = 6%.


As you calculate, take into account these three questions:


1.


**Are you excluding short abandons?** Most teams ignore hang-ups in the first 5 to 10 seconds, since those are usually misdials.[SQM Group](https://www.sqmgroup.com/resources/library/blog/call-abandonment-rate-comprehensive-guide) estimates these false abandons can make up as much as 2% of call volume, which is enough to push a healthy line into the warning zone on paper.


2.


**Does IVR abandonment count?** A caller who gives up three menus deep is often just as frustrated, if not more, as one who gives up in the queue. We recommend tracking IVR abandonments, even if you report them separately.


3.


**What’s your denominator?** We recommend using calls offered, meaning every call that reached your system, as opposed to only the calls that made it to an agent queue. Otherwise, you’re hiding callers your routing lost before then.


## What is a normal call abandonment rate?


Most industry benchmarks put the average between 5% and 8%.[SQM Group](https://www.sqmgroup.com/resources/library/blog/call-abandonment-rate-comprehensive-guide) puts the industry benchmark at 5% and finds that contact centers with the strongest customer satisfaction tend to run at 3% or less.


Here’s how to read your number:


**Abandonment rate**


**What it usually means**


Under 3%


Top tier. Typical of contact centers with the highest customer satisfaction.


3% to 5%


Good. Your capacity is keeping up with demand.


5% to 8%


Average. Acceptable for many operations, but you’re still losing customers you could keep.


8% to 10%


Warning. Staffing, routing, or wait times need attention.


Over 10%


High. Callers are routinely giving up before you can help them.


Take into account that these benchmarks often also shift by industry. Healthcare lines, for example, average around 7% according to[Sprinklr](https://www.sprinklr.com/blog/call-center-statistics/) , driven by complex questions and longer calls.


One note on outbound: abandonment means something different when you’re the one dialing. For outbound campaigns, an abandoned call is one where the customer picks up and no agent is there. US telemarketing rules cap that at 3%, which makes it a compliance metric rather than a customer experience one. In this post, we’re focusing solely on inbound.


## Why the average hides the real problem


A 6% monthly average sounds fine, but it could break down to 2% one day, and 20% another. Averages flatten peaks, but peaks are the signals that something’s gone wrong.


Two cuts tell you far more than the headline number:


1.


**By time:** Break abandonment out by hour, day, and season. If the spikes line up with your busiest weeks, your problem probably isn’t service quality: it’s concurrency.


2.


**By intent:** Abandonment on a support line costs you a callback, while abandonment on a sales line costs you the sale, and probably the customer.


## What causes high call abandonment?


Most abandonment comes down to a handful of things:


1.


**Long wait times:** This is often the single biggest driver, with every extra minute in the queue leading to more calls abandoned.


2.


**Understaffing during peaks:** Forecasts miss, volume surges, and your team is in trouble.


3.


**IVR friction:** Deep menus and “press 1 for” mazes lose callers before they ever reach your queue.


4.


**No visibility:** Callers who don’t know how long they’ll be waiting tend to assume the worst.


5.


**No callback option:** A callback gives callers a way out of a long hold while still getting help. Without one, hanging up is their only exit.


## How to reduce call abandonment rate


The standard playbook is well known: forecast and staff more precisely, offer callbacks, announce wait times, streamline IVRs, and improve first call resolution. All of it helps, but none of it solves the underlying problem: if you’re relying on human agents only at your call center, your workflow is set by limited resources.


When you have more callers than agents, potential customers have to wait. Some of them, eventually, hang up.


This is one of the clearest benefits of voice AI. AI agents answer on the first ring, and are capable of handling a large share of calls end to end. The queue that used to form in front of your agents either gets shorter, or never forms at all.


## How Omaha Steaks went from 16% to 2%


Two years ago, 16% of callers to Omaha Steaks hung up before reaching their agents. Last year, the number was 9%. Today? It’s 2%, measured across a line that handles 12 times its normal volume in December. That’s top-tier performance by any benchmark, on one of the hardest seasonal curves in retail.[Read the full Omaha Steaks story](https://www.usesimple.ai/blog/how-omaha-steaks-cut-call-abandonment-from-16-to-3) .


Three things changed when they started working with Simple:


1.


**Every call gets answered immediately.** Our AI agent picks up on the first ring, no matter the season. December’s surge no longer turns into a December queue.


2.


**Most callers never need the queue.** With 72% of calls fully handled by Simone, the customers who do need a live agent join a much shorter line.


3.


**The callers who wait, happily wait longer.** This last one surprised even us. Callers who talked to an AI agent before holding for a human stayed on the line about 30 seconds longer than they had prior. Being greeted, understood, and in the know made customers more patient overall.


What does that look like on a sales line? If yours takes 10,000 calls a week at peak, 16% abandonment means 1,600 callers hang up. At 2%, it’s 200. That’s 1,400 more customers per week, reaching someone ready to take their order.


## Every abandoned call is a customer who wanted something


Maybe they wanted to place an order, or maybe they had a problem you could fix. Regardless, they gave up because nobody was there.


We think that’s a solvable problem. Nobody should have to wait in line to be helped, and with the right voice AI solution, nobody has to. With Simple, service starts on the very first ring.
